description: A group consisting of children who ask AI to help identify locations on Earth that are analogous to potential permanent base sites on the Moon or Mars.
summary: Team GetHub created an interactive browser expedition that puts young explorers in charge of choosing Earth-based rehearsals for the Moon and Mars. Players read field evidence, compare terrains and record recommendations in a mission journal. Cinder Lake and Haughton demonstrate established uses of analog sites. Santa Marta, an impact crater in Piauí, Brazil, is examined as a candidate for practising how to map an eroded crater rim. The game helps players connect published evidence to a specific field task and identify what a team still needs to measure.
details:
We built a browser game inspired by Jules Verne with three guided stops, three selectable crew guides and a nine-site atlas. At each stop, players open two clues, compare Earth observations with a lunar or Martian reference and choose a field test. Feedback and a downloadable field journal connect each decision to the evidence and its limits.

For the Santa Marta case, we compare published crater diameters in kilometres: Santa Marta, approximately 10; Haughton, an estimated original rim of 23–24; Shackleton, 21; and Jezero, 45. We calculate the absolute difference from each planetary target and preserve Haughton’s reported range. Haughton is closer to both targets in diameter. Oliveira and colleagues mapped a central plateau about 3.2 km across and reported an elevation difference of nearly 200 m between sectors of Santa Marta’s western and eastern rims. These observations support considering Santa Marta for a terrain-mapping exercise. A rover route still needs measurements of slope and surface roughness plus a check of field access.

The game uses HTML, CSS and JavaScript with embedded illustrations, progress stored in the browser, downloadable data and an optional NASA POWER climate lookup. NASA and ESA resources give players evidence from Earth, the Moon and Mars. The game shows how evidence supports a particular training task and what further measurements would be needed.

Team GetHub selected the challenge, the Jules Verne concept and the research materials. ChatGPT Codex and Claude assisted with research, game design, code, analysis and English text. OpenAI image generation supplied the labelled cover and explorer portraits. The game and demonstration credit AI-assisted work and identify the published sources of scientific measurements.
